picks.name: The Fitness Enthusiast
picks.why_plausible: Works out 4+ times a week and already buys supplements and recovery products, so protein bars are a standing replenishment purchase; price_sensitivity low-medium and AOV $88 make a $35 box trivial.
lean_into: brand loyalty to things that perform
avoid: implying the bar is a treat instead of fuel
picks.ad_angle: The post-workout bar you'll actually look forward to — same protein numbers, none of the chalk.

picks.name: The Wellness Optimizer
picks.why_plausible: Tracks supplements and workouts and pays premiums for good products (price_sensitivity: low, wellness/supplements affinities), so a protein bar is already in her rotation. Her disinterest in 'ultra-processed food' means the ad must lean on ingredients rather than candy-bar framing.
lean_into: outcome-focused: protein per bar that fits her macros
a bar that tastes good without being a candy bar
avoid: unbacked science-y claims the brand can't support
picks.ad_angle: Hitting your protein target shouldn't mean choking down chalk — a clean-ingredient bar you'll finish.

picks.name: The Convenience-First Millennial
picks.why_plausible: Heavy subscription user with snack-replenishment behavior (affinities: quick_commerce, subscription_services) and AOV $55, so a restockable desk/bag snack is an easy default buy.
picks.ad_angle: The default snack in your drawer — auto-restocked, and the one you don't dread eating.

picks.name: The Gen Z Aesthete
picks.why_plausible: Her messaging_preferences literally include 'playful' and 'novelty', matching the brand's playful value, and functional_beverages affinity shows she buys better-for-you snackables at ~$48 AOV.
avoid: dry performance claims with no vibe
picks.ad_angle: A protein bar with a sense of humor — led by flavor and brand voice, not gym talk.

picks.name: The Busy Parent
picks.why_plausible: Time-poor dual-income household that buys in bulk and loves subscriptions; protein bars are a lunchbox/car staple, and 'tastes good' is exactly the claim that gets a snack eaten instead of thrown out.
lean_into: family-friendly, kids will actually eat it
picks.ad_angle: The protein bar that comes home empty — a bulk-box staple kids and adults both finish.

plan.summary: Budget leans to fitness-intent and consumable-replenishment checkouts (Studiogrid, Movewell, Daily Form, Pop & Sip) where a $35 bar box is a same-size add-on, with tests on high-reach food and convenience baskets (Swiftcart, Kitchenly, Pantrygood) and all pet, beauty, home and non-fitness apparel excluded for lacking any purchase-level link.

recommended.name: Daily Form
recommended.tier_reason: The score treated this as a loose supplement adjacency, but the purchase moment is exact: someone who just bought a vitamin/supplement subscription is a habitual buyer of consumable health products, and a protein bar is the obvious next replenishment at a near-identical basket size ($35 vs $38). The notes' skepticism warning targets health claims, and this brand's pitch is taste, not efficacy.
recommended.rationale: Shoppers here sell-through on consumable wellness replenishment ('vitamins', 'supplements', 'subscription') at $38 orders, so a $35 bar box is a same-size, same-habit follow-on; the taste-first claim sidesteps the audience being 'skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims'.

evidence.quote: Audience skeptical of unsubstantiated health claims

recommended.risk: 89% female, science-forward audience may want macros and ingredient substantiation the 'tastes good' pitch doesn't provide; 4.2M impressions caps volume.

recommended.name: Movewell
recommended.tier_reason: Computed as test on category overlap alone, but the notes name the exact buyer: 'Fitness-engaged shoppers' just buying activewear are the people who already keep protein bars in the bag, and at 22M impressions this can carry core budget.
recommended.rationale: Notes describe 'Fitness-engaged shoppers', and a $35 bar box is a light add-on against a $78 activewear basket — a natural fuel purchase for someone kitting out their training.
recommended.risk: Activewear buying is episodic and fashion-led; some of these shoppers are buying leggings for style, not training.

recommended.name: Studiogrid
recommended.tier_reason: The score gave zero on values and read this as generic wellness, but the notes make the intent explicit — these users are booking and paying for workouts right now, which is the sharpest possible moment to offer post-workout fuel at a matched basket size.
recommended.rationale: Notes say users are 'actively spending on self-care and fitness' via appointment booking, so a protein bar is the natural companion to a just-booked class, and $35 sits just under the $42 typical order.

evidence.quote: Users are actively spending on self-care and fitness

recommended.risk: Spa and yoga bookings dilute the training-fuel intent, and a high-income 28-50 audience may skew to premium/whole-food snacking.

recommended.name: Pop & Sip
recommended.tier_reason: Tags only saw a weak wellness/functional-beverage link, but the notes describe this brand's exact positioning: 'Health-curious but indulgence-seeking' is precisely the shopper who wants protein that doesn't taste like cardboard.
recommended.rationale: The notes' 'Health-curious but indulgence-seeking' buyer is the target for a taste-first protein bar, and a $35 offer fits neatly under the $42 functional-beverage basket as a pantry add-on.
recommended.risk: Only 5.2M impressions, so volume is limited even at a good conversion rate; gut-health framing may pull toward ingredient claims this brand doesn't make.

test.name: Pantrygood
test.tier_reason: Excluded on a low values score, but the record shows a real snack-replenishment basket: 'pantry' and 'subscription' grocery shoppers restock consumables, and a bar box is a natural line item. The open question is whether a taste-first pitch lands on an audience the notes call clean-ingredient driven.
test.rationale: Pantry/subscription grocery buyers restock snacks on a cycle, but the notes say they are 'Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims' — claims this brand doesn't make — so this is worth a measured test rather than core budget.

evidence.quote: Responsive to clean-ingredient, sustainability, and wellness claims

test.risk: An organic/natural grocer may already stock competing bars, so the offer can read as redundant; $86 baskets also mean the shopper just spent heavily on food.

test.name: Swiftcart
test.tier_reason: Excluded as weak fit despite matching the advertiser's own snacks, impulse and replenishment signals at 84M impressions and a $28 basket — the largest impulse-snack moment in the catalog. Test rather than recommend because late-night convenience orders skew indulgent and the retailer may already carry bars.
test.rationale: Notes describe 'High-frequency purchasers' who are 'Impulse-friendly' with a $28 typical order, so a $35 bar box is a plausible impulse add-on at huge scale; what needs measuring is whether late-night snack buyers convert on a multi-bar box.
test.risk: Late-night alcohol/convenience traffic is indulgence-led, and a convenience grocery app likely stocks competing bars the shopper can add to the next order instead.

test.name: Kitchenly
test.tier_reason: Excluded on weak tag overlap, but meal-kit subscribers are the clearest 'food-interested' cohort in the catalog and buy recurring food subscriptions already; the taste claim is aimed exactly at people who care how food tastes. Test because the household/family basket may want snacks for kids rather than protein.
test.rationale: Notes call these shoppers 'Convenience-motivated but food-interested' subscription buyers, so a recurring, good-tasting protein snack is a credible next subscription at 36M impressions.
test.risk: A $74 dinner-solution basket signals cooked meals, not grab-and-go fuel; the 28-52 family audience may not be protein-bar buyers at all.

launch_summary.summary: $8,500 goes to four core checkouts split evenly — Studiogrid, Movewell, Daily Form and Pop & Sip — where fitness intent or consumable restocking makes a $35 bar box a same-size add-on. A $1,500 test budget across Pantrygood, Swiftcart and Kitchenly asks whether high-reach food and convenience baskets convert on a multi-bar box, or whether those shoppers already buy competing bars nearby. All five personas, from The Fitness Enthusiast to The Busy Parent, run across most placements; pet, beauty, home and non-fitness apparel were excluded.
uncertainties: The $35 first order value is assumed, and the $12.25 target and $15.93 maximum cost per new customer are built on it.
The business model is unknown, so the 35% allowable ratio stands in for real margin and lifetime value.
The 25-45, any-gender audience is assumed, and the grocery and meal-kit tests may reach shoppers who aren't protein-bar buyers at all.
questions: What is your actual average first order value and margin on it?
Do you sell mainly one-time boxes, subscriptions, or both?
Do you make clean-ingredient or sustainability claims, which the Pantrygood audience responds to?
